<reason>CON (A) framed the motion as a substitution test from the opening ("excellent supplement, hollow substitute") and then tracked PRO's concessions round by round: persistent presence moves to a full-time CERT, a "coordination core is useful," and foreign collection/disruption "can remain with existing national authorities." A's weighing rule—"you rely on the thing whose absence loses the contest"—combined with the concrete point that utility staff exist regardless of a reserve program and only see their own logs, not the campaign, left PRO's "presence on the terrain is reliance" looking thin. PRO's best move was the legitimate reframe that the motion names military units, not any standing body (sharp Q1), and A's slide from "military" to "military and intelligence" was a real vulnerability; but PRO never explained how a civilian agency lawfully conducts foreign collection or why the country isn't still relying on the retained authorities for the decisive functions. A's three clipped turns are an execution cost but did not remove core content. Clear but competitive win for A.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 answer to B's Q2 plus the surrounding weighing: seeing the adversary's side means intrusion into foreign infrastructure, routed through sovereign bodies; a civilian agency tasking insiders "inherits the insiders' blind spot"; and PRO has "built the standing units twice" under new labels. Paired with seizing B4.3's "existing national authorities" concession, this materially damaged PRO's claim to have replaced rather than renamed standing units.</best_rebuttal>
